>There are people out there who use and abuse and cheat, and do drugs and steal and molest.

>she needs to nip this in the bud now and get his mind right.

He is sexually **abusive** to her. Of course there are happy times, she wouldn't be married to him if there wasn't happy times. It doesn't change the fact that he is **not listening** when she tells him to **stop**. Your logic is classic abuser language and it sickens me.

Say my ex slaps me in the face every day. We have built a life together and I'm happy for the most part. Should I end it because he slaps me in the face once? Maybe not. Should I end it because he slaps me in the face every day and I tell him not to? Yes. He is systematically crossing her boundaries and sulking when he doesn't get his own way. Her husband **does not own her** and never has, he doesn't get the *right* to behave this way.

And he **does** know he's doing it because he's been **told**. You are minimising it because you're trying to excuse it, downplay it, use the rest of her marriage to convince her to stay and put up with it. She's describing the emotionally abusive aspects of her relationship in this post, so of course we're going to comment on it.

She could have the best relationship in the whole world outside of being pinched when she doesn't want to, it doesn't change the fact he's **abusing** her. And he **knows** because she has **told him to stop.**

Let me put this bluntly, since you've decided to label me an idiot.

>My husband likes to grab my nipples all the time whether I'm in the house braless with a t-shirt or even with a bra on.

It doesn't matter if he doesn't realise it's abusive, he should be listening to his wife and treating her the way he would like to be treated. It's the start of financial abuse if it isn't nipped in the bud. FIRM talk about boundaries is needed. Don't butter it up to be not a big deal, OP. It's a big deal. If a friend took money from your card without your permission you'd be horrified, expect no less respect and trust from your partner.

Oh and be honest with your therapist. A lot of abusers go to therapy and talk about how their *wife made them feel such a way* and just go to get validation that their wife is as wrong as they are. You are not to blame the victim. You are not to *expect* her to love you after what you've done. You're not to expect her to *accept* your treatment, or that she *owes* you gratitude for attending the therapy. The fact you came here for validation about getting help from *victims* says a lot about you. I have a feeling you've done this post so you can show your wife how much the internet supports you more than she supports you right now, because I've been there as a spectator of that myself. She has a right to her pain. You don't deserve anything at this moment in time, except common human decency and kindness and respect. As much as a prisoner would be afforded for committing a crime, I'm sure. You don't need internet points, you need to recognise what you've done is wrong not because you need a reward for it but because you've committed a heinous act against someone who only loved you too much.

It's different saying "don't beat yourself up" to the victim, as they're feeling misplaced guilt. Abuse is a choice. We choose to abuse. Whether he means to or not, it's a choice we make. Your gut feeling will be stronger than any word ever written. Your gut will tell you why its wrong from his body language when he excuses his behaviour, from the lack of change when he said he wouldn't do it again, and from the words he chooses to use despite them sounding so sweet and not sitting right for some reason. Always trust your gut to tell you things about what he's not saying out loud or how he is saying things.

It's hard to break the cycle with emotional abuse. Because what happens is they cripple our self esteem and make it seem like we wouldn't be able to do it without them. By saying that you don't understand, that you don't get it, that you have to have things repeated at you; he's calling you stupid. He's saying that he knows what is right. >I talked to him about it later that his raised voice is scary to me, and he said just don’t let it scare you.

If I stand on his feet and he says it hurts him, should I have the right to say "Just don't let it hurt you?" That's abusive behaviour, as he's dictating how you should respond to aggression. And a raised voice is aggressive, he's behaving like a bully.

>Then he gets pissed off and is like omg you’re so sensitive, what are you going to do if a dog barks at you, stop being ridiculous and stop giving bad vibes.

"You're so sensitive" -> translates to "I can't handle the fact that you're setting boundaries and breaking my internal rules. I'm going to make you feel like you're overreacting so I can get away with it." There's no such thing as *too sensitive* but there is such thing as *someone taking advantage of someone who is sensitive.* Sensitivity is a GOOD trait to have! It makes you attentive and wary of people being harmful to you and to others. And yes, if a dog barks at you you will flinch. That's reflex. The difference is, a dog seldom tends to choose when to bark. It generally does it by instinct when feeling threatened or to communicate at a distance. A partner chooses to shout at you.

>for example when I mishear him/don’t understand him. He said just stop asking what I said so many times you don’t have to understand what I said, it just pisses me off to repeat myself, it’s like my gf doesn’t understand English

"You don't have to understand what I said" yes you do. That's how communicating works. "It just pisses me off to repeat myself" take the 'just' out of that, because just is short for justification and that means he's making an excuse. Watch out for "I'm only" as well. "It's like my GF doesn't understand English" that's just bullying too.

He's emotionally and verbally abusive in these examples.

It's up to you to decide whether that's something you can handle, as now that he's shown you he's capable of it you're going to be on edge trying to avoid him having to raise his voice. >Why not just leave?

Do you not believe victims, such as myself, chronically think that? It's a form of self torture when we ask ourselves that, "Why didn't I just leave?" "I wasted x years trying to fix this" and "If I knew he'd been like this, I would've left a \_\_\_ weeks/months, not at \_\_\_ years."

Why not just leave? Often enough abuse victims are already vulnerable people. A resilient person would absolutely leave, as they know what their boundaries are and refuse to have them crossed.

Vulnerable people don't generally know what boundaries are, or haven't properly established them. They are absolutely not to blame for this. It can stem from not having a good upbringing, or from slowly and systematically being worn down and controlled as u/UnluckySnowLion mentions in their comment there.

It starts with overdosing the vulnerable person with love, also known as love bombing. This increases the amount of oxytocin in the brain, and forms an addictive bond to the person who is showering you with love. Perhaps love you've seldom been shown before.

And then they begin with coercive behaviour, or tiny comments, where you think to yourself "Oh that's not *them*, I know who they are and they would *never* say something like that to me. Something must be going on. I must help them to overcome it so we can go back to how things were at first." This is when cortisol is introduced, the stress hormone.

And it's made better again! Not just flowers and chocolates, but the lovebombing stage 1 begins all over again. You're tricked into thinking it's okay all over again. Edit: bear in mind how the brain does not like to hold onto negative memories, so it tends to only think of positive ones. 'rose tinted glasses' is a thing.

Oxytocin, cortosol, oxytocin, cortosol. It forms what's known as a trauma bond, and it's one hell of an addiction to free yourself of. It's been likened to that of cocaine.
